sections.heading: Quick answer
paragraphs: > **Quick answer:** A Lilly savings program is not one universal offer. Lilly Cares is charitable patient assistance for qualifying U.S. patients and listed medications, while a Mounjaro Savings Card is a separate commercial program. Check the exact medication, insurance lane, income or eligibility rules, limits, and current terms before comparing amounts. [S1][S2][S3]

sections.heading: What “Lilly savings program” can mean
paragraphs: Searchers often use one phrase for several different ways of reducing a prescription cost. The first question is not “What is the discount?” It is “Which program is being described, for which medication, and for which insurance situation?” A nonprofit patient-assistance program, a manufacturer commercial card, a self-pay price, an insurance benefit, and an alternate-funding process are different mechanisms.

That distinction matters because the same manufacturer can publish multiple programs at once. A page describing Lilly Cares may discuss qualifying patients receiving prescribed Lilly medications at no cost, while a product page may describe a card that reduces a commercial pharmacy claim. Those statements are not interchangeable, and one should not be used to infer the eligibility or amount in another lane. [S1][S3]

This guide uses current official Lilly pages checked on August 22, 2026. It is a source-based navigation guide, not a personal eligibility screen. Program terms, medication lists, prices, insurance rules, and pharmacy results can change. The relevant plan, pharmacy, manufacturer page, and healthcare team remain the places to verify a person’s current circumstances.

sections.heading: What Lilly Cares currently is
paragraphs: The Lilly Cares Foundation describes its Patient Assistance Program as a nonprofit charitable organization that provides prescribed Lilly medications for free for up to 12 months to qualifying U.S. patients. That is the defining charitable-assistance lane in this comparison. It is not the same as a general coupon or a promise that every Lilly medication is available through the program. [S1]

The current How to Apply page states that a person may be eligible only when a healthcare provider has prescribed a medication offered through Lilly Cares and the person meets the program’s residence, insurance, medication-specific, and household-income requirements. The page also lists restrictions involving Medicaid, full Low Income Subsidy or Extra Help, Veterans benefits, and certain alternative-funding arrangements. [S2]

The current page organizes its medication list into groups with different insurance and income rules. The displayed list includes products such as Trulicity, several insulin products, Ebglyss, Taltz, and other named medicines. The listed group thresholds are not a universal rule for every Lilly product or every applicant; the medication group and the application requirements control the relevant lane. [S2]

sections.heading: Check the exact medication before applying
paragraphs: The fastest way to avoid a wrong answer is to check the current Lilly Cares medication list before comparing income thresholds or assuming that a product has charitable assistance. The current page reviewed for this refresh does not list Mounjaro or Zepbound in the displayed medication groups. That is a bounded observation about the current page, not a claim that no other assistance resource exists. [S2] For a “tirzepatide patient assistance program” search, verify the exact brand and current medication list: Mounjaro is tirzepatide, but the current Lilly Cares list reviewed here does not name Mounjaro and directs unlisted medications to the Medicine Assistance Tool. [S2][S3] If the medication is not listed, the same page directs readers to the Medicine Assistance Tool for additional resources. That referral is a routing instruction, not an approval, price quote, or guarantee that another program will accept an application. Use it to continue research only after confirming the medication name, the patient’s insurance lane, and the date of the terms being reviewed. [S2]

This medication-list check is the key answer to a common search-intent question: “Can I use Lilly Cares for this product?” The answer cannot be produced from the manufacturer name alone. Verify the exact product and presentation against the live list, then read the applicable application and insurance-document requirements. Do not substitute a different Lilly product because it appears in the list.

sections.heading: How the Lilly Cares application works
paragraphs: Choose an application.

The current Lilly Cares page offers three application paths: an online application, a downloadable paper application completed by hand or on a computer, and a mailed application request by phone. The page says the online option reduces paperwork and potential delays. [S21]
Complete and submit.

The current instructions say the patient completes and signs the patient sections, the healthcare provider completes the prescriber section and submits a prescription, and the completed online or paper application is submitted through the stated online, fax, or mail path. [S10]
What happens next.

Lilly Cares says it reviews the application and sends an enrollment decision to the patient and healthcare provider. If approved, the notification states the enrollment expiration; medications are shipped to the home or healthcare provider’s office, and reapplication is required at the end of the enrollment period. [S10]

sections.heading: Mounjaro commercial savings is a separate lane
paragraphs: The current Mounjaro Savings & Coverage page describes a commercial savings card, not Lilly Cares charitable assistance. For eligible patients with commercial drug insurance that covers Mounjaro, the page says the patient may pay as little as $25 for a 1-, 2-, or 3-month prescription fill, subject to the card terms. It defines one month as 28 days and up to four single-dose pens, with separate maximum monthly and annual savings limits. The card expires and savings end on December 31, 2026. [S3][S19]

The covered-commercial-insurance example is not a universal $25 price. The same terms require commercial drug insurance that covers Mounjaro, an approved-use prescription consistent with FDA-approved labeling, and other eligibility conditions. The page specifies maximum monthly savings of up to $150 for a 1-month fill, $300 for a 2-month fill, or $450 for a 3-month fill, plus a separate maximum annual savings of up to $1,950 and a maximum of up to 13 prescription fills per calendar year. The terms also say card eligibility and terms may be terminated, rescinded, revoked, or amended by Lilly at any time without notice or for any reason. [S3]

The page also describes a different commercial-insurance situation: patients with commercial drug insurance that does not cover Mounjaro may pay as little as $499 for a 1-month prescription fill, subject to the card’s requirements and limits. The same lane has maximum savings of up to $647 per month, up to $8,411 per calendar year, and up to 13 prescription fills per calendar year. That is a separate card lane from the covered-commercial-insurance example. It should not be presented as a Lilly Cares grant, a Medicare benefit, or an amount available to every uninsured patient. The card expires and savings end on December 31, 2026. [S3][S19]

The Mounjaro terms state that card savings cannot be combined with another program, discount, discount card, cash discount card, coupon, incentive, or similar offer involving Mounjaro. The terms also state that the card is not insurance. A card can change the patient’s out-of-pocket result without becoming an insurance policy or charitable-assistance award. [S3]
When comparing manufacturer pages, preserve the labels exactly:

sections.heading: Other Lilly affordability program pages
paragraphs: Lilly runs separate program pages for other medicines: a general access-and-affordability resources hub, the Lilly Insulin Value Program, and Foundayo coverage and savings, which covers self-pay, commercial-insurance, and Medicare Part D navigation. The pages reviewed for this guide state only these program headings and do not state product-specific prices or eligibility. [S5][S7][S8] Keep these as separate program pages rather than treating every Lilly affordability result as one combined offer.

sections.heading: List price, self-pay, insurance, and final amount
paragraphs: Lilly’s Mounjaro cost-information page lists a $1,112.16 per-fill list price. The page says the amount a patient pays will largely depend on the prescription drug insurance plan and that specific insurance-plan pricing is not yet available on that page. A list price is a reference figure, not a patient-specific pharmacy quote. [S4]

The same page says commercially insured patients may be eligible for the Mounjaro Savings Card, while people whose commercial or government insurance does not cover Mounjaro, or people with no insurance, may be eligible for self-pay savings options. The wording is conditional. It does not turn the list price, a savings-card number, or a self-pay option into a guaranteed final amount. [S4]

Lilly also explains that pharmacy prices can differ from list price and can depend on out-of-pocket costs set by the insurer, pharmacy charges, and discounts or financial assistance available to the patient. Keep those components separate when making a comparison. The reviewed source does not state a patient-specific final amount. [S4]

paragraphs: The current Lilly Cares application page and Mounjaro cost-information page describe different program boundaries. Lilly Cares lists insurance and alternative-funding requirements as part of charitable-assistance eligibility. The Mounjaro cost page states that patients with Medicaid, Medicare, Medigap, DoD, VA, TRICARE or CHAMPUS, or a state patient or pharmaceutical assistance program are not eligible for the Mounjaro Savings Program. Treat these as lane-specific manufacturer statements, not as a universal rule for every affordability resource. [S2][S4]

The Lilly Cares page also describes alternative funding programs, for-profit patient advocacy programs, and specialty cost-containment networks as arrangements that can affect eligibility. Do not assume that a patient can simply stack a charitable application, an insurer requirement, and a manufacturer card. If a person is covered by a government program, the correct next step is not to replace that coverage with a commercial-card assumption. Verify the plan’s formulary, benefit rules, appeals or assistance pathways, and any applicable manufacturer restrictions through the relevant official channels. sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Mistake 1: Treating every Lilly offer as Lilly Cares.

A manufacturer can operate a nonprofit foundation and separate commercial product pages. The fact that both use Lilly branding does not make their terms interchangeable. Identify the program name in the source and keep charitable assistance separate from a card, coupon, or self-pay option.
Mistake 2: Using a headline number without its insurance condition.

“$25” and “$499” are not free-floating prices. They appear in specific Mounjaro commercial-card lanes with eligibility, coverage, fill definitions, savings caps, and annual limits. Record the insurance condition next to any number or the comparison is incomplete. [S3]
Mistake 3: Calling a list price the amount a patient will pay.

A list price can provide context, but the patient’s amount depends on the transaction and applicable insurance, charges, discounts, or assistance. A public list-price page cannot adjudicate an individual pharmacy claim. [S4]
Mistake 4: Assuming that “not listed” means “no help exists anywhere”.

A medication absent from the current Lilly Cares list should not be treated as approved through Lilly Cares. It also should not be turned into a universal statement that no other resource exists. The current page directs readers to the Medicine Assistance Tool for additional resources. [S2]
Mistake 5: Combining lanes without checking the terms.

The Mounjaro card terms state that card savings cannot be combined with similar Mounjaro discounts or offers. Other assistance programs can have their own restrictions. Compare eligibility and stacking rules before assuming that two offers can be used together. [S3]

articles.conclusion: A responsible counterfeit Ozempic check uses layers: current FDA warning identifiers, the bounded EXP/LOT placement comparison, the dispensing pharmacy's legal identity and state license, preserved package and transaction evidence, manufacturer or pharmacy contact, and the FDA route matched to the issue. A warning match requires following FDA's instruction not to use, distribute, or sell the identified product. A nonmatch is not proof of authenticity. Keep uncertainty explicit, preserve original evidence, and record official case numbers. The current FDA pages control the latest warning and reporting instructions, not a seller, social post, or price.

articles.direct_answer: FDA has warned about counterfeit Ozempic found in the U.S. drug supply chain and tells patients, pharmacies, and other supply-chain participants to check products, avoid using, distributing, or selling products labeled with the identified counterfeit information, and report concerns through the appropriate official channel. The current warning identifies specific lot and serial information and one visible placement difference for the EXP/LOT text. Those checks are stop signals, not a universal authenticity certificate: a package that doesn't match one warning can still require verification. Start with the dispensing channel, confirm that the pharmacy is state licensed, preserve the packaging and transaction record, contact the dispensing pharmacy or manufacturer for authenticity concerns, and use FDA reporting routes that match the event. The evidence process does not diagnose an exposure, determine whether a product is authentic, or recommend treatment.

sections.h2: What the current FDA warning establishes
paragraphs: A suspect Ozempic package calls for documentation, not a visual guess. FDA has identified counterfeit product in the U.S. drug supply chain and published specific lot, serial, and package-placement information. A match is a stop signal; a nonmatch is not a universal authenticity certificate. Preserve the package and transaction record, trace the dispensing channel, verify the pharmacy, and use the official reporting route that fits the concern.

The same warning tells people not to use, distribute, or sell products labeled with the counterfeit information identified by FDA. It reports uncertainty about the seized products' identity, quality, and safety and notes an increased infection risk from counterfeit needles. The cited evidence does not extend those statements to every Ozempic pen or predict what any specific suspect product contains. Its job is narrower: preserve the identifiers FDA published, show how to separate a warning match from a broader verification decision, and route documentation to official channels without creating a fake consumer certification system.

The current FDA warning lists three affected lot numbers: PAR1229, PAR0362, and NAR0074. It also identifies serial information beginning with 51746517 and the specific serial number 430834149057. Copy the characters exactly as printed, including their order, rather than relying on memory or a cropped marketplace image. Record where each identifier appears on the carton or pen, the expiration information beside it, the product description, and the quantity received. A clear photograph of the full face plus close images of each identifier creates a more useful record than a typed number alone.

An identifier match is a stop signal under the warning. It is not permission to keep using the product while waiting for informal confirmation, and it is not something a seller can neutralize with a text message. Conversely, an identifier that doesn't match this list is not proof that the package is authentic. FDA warnings describe evidence known at a point in time; counterfeiters can change numbers, labels, and channels. Reopen the current FDA warning when checking a real product because the agency can update identifiers, images, instructions, or the investigation status after the cited evidence's July 23, 2026 source check.

sections.h2: Copy the lot, serial, and package details exactly
paragraphs: FDA describes a visible placement difference in the affected products. On the counterfeit products in the warning, the EXP/LOT text appears on the left side of the expiration date and lot number. FDA says authentic Ozempic pens have the EXP/LOT text above the expiration date and lot number. Photograph the relevant panel straight on, in enough light to read the text, without editing or applying filters. Preserve a wider image showing which package or pen the close-up belongs to. That reduces the chance that a detached image is later confused with another item.

Treat this as a warning-specific comparison, not a complete authentication test. Packaging can vary by market, product presentation, and time, and FDA doesn't say that one layout check proves every other feature is genuine. Do not invent additional telltales from color, font weight, needle appearance, box texture, or online side-by-side graphics unless a current cited source supports them. A mismatch can justify escalation; a match to one expected feature doesn't close the case. Channel, license, reviewed sources, manufacturer contact, and current FDA information remain part of the evidence decision.

sections.h2: Trace the product back to the dispensing pharmacy
paragraphs: FDA's counterfeit-medicine guidance says consumers should buy from state-licensed pharmacies. The current Ozempic warning also says Ozempic should be obtained only with a valid prescription through state-licensed pharmacies. Record the pharmacy's legal name, physical location, website or app used, prescription record, order date, transaction amount, and dispensing label. A brand-like website name is not the same thing as a pharmacy license. A telehealth intake, marketplace listing, social account, payment link, or shipping label also doesn't substitute for the dispensing pharmacy's identity and license status.

Use the FDA BeSafeRx state-license path to reach the relevant state board of pharmacy record, then compare the legal business name and location with the dispensing information. Check both the state where the pharmacy operates and the requirements relevant to the buyer's state. Save the result date and the record used. A license record is strong channel evidence but still doesn't authenticate one physical package. If the seller will not identify the dispensing pharmacy, the license can't be found, or the names and locations don't reconcile, preserve that discrepancy instead of filling the gap with a guess.

A useful record can be small: full carton photographs, pen photographs, close images of lot, serial, expiration, and EXP/LOT placement, the dispensing label with unnecessary personal details redacted for sharing, receipt or transaction record, pharmacy legal name, state-license lookup result, order and delivery dates, seller or platform URL, and a short factual timeline. Keep the original files. If creating a review copy, note what was redacted or resized. Do not alter the identifiers, replace backgrounds, or combine images in a way that hides which surface they came from.

Write observations, not conclusions. For example: 'Carton shows lot PAR1229; photograph captured July 23' is stronger than 'This is definitely fake' unless a cited source has made that determination. 'EXP/LOT text appears to the left of the date' is more reviewable than 'Packaging looks wrong.' Record who dispensed the product and which official page was checked. Keep seller promises, chats, or advertisements as separate evidence. This structure lets the pharmacy, manufacturer, FDA, or another authorized reviewer inspect the same facts without depending on the consumer's theory.

sections.h2: When the warning information matches
paragraphs: FDA's instruction is direct: don't use, distribute, or sell products labeled with the counterfeit information in the warning. Keep the item and packaging available for the next official instruction rather than passing it to another person or returning it through an unverified seller workflow that could put it back into circulation. Contact the dispensing pharmacy and explain the exact lot, serial, and packaging observations. FDA's warning also gives Novo Nordisk customer care as a contact for authenticity concerns. Record the date, channel, case number, and factual response from each contact.

The cited evidence does not provide storage, handling, disposal, replacement, or medical instructions for a suspect product. Those depend on current direction from the dispensing pharmacy, manufacturer, FDA, or an appropriate licensed professional. It also doesn't tell a person whether an observed event came from a counterfeit product. If there is an adverse event or side-effect concern, FDA provides the MedWatch reporting program; the report should describe what happened and identify the suspect product without asking an informational summary to interpret causation. Preserve official case numbers so later reports can be connected accurately.

sections.h2: Choose the reporting route that fits the concern
paragraphs: FDA identifies several routes with different purposes. Suspected counterfeit products can be reported to a local FDA consumer complaint coordinator. Adverse events or side effects can be reported through the MedWatch Safety Information and Adverse Event Reporting Program; the current warning says reports can be submitted online or by fax to 1-800-FDA-0178. FDA's counterfeit-medicine guidance also points to reporting unsafe online pharmacy sales and suspected criminal counterfeit activity through the appropriate FDA channels. Don't assume that one report automatically performs every other function.

Match the record to the route. A product complaint should foreground identifiers, packaging, channel, license, and transaction evidence. An unsafe online pharmacy report should preserve the website, seller identity, claimed pharmacy, payment path, prescription behavior, and license discrepancy. A MedWatch report should follow the program's requested event and product fields rather than turning a packaging concern into an unsupported medical conclusion. Criminal-activity reporting should preserve seller communications and transaction facts. Save submission confirmations and report numbers; they are evidence that a route was used, not proof of FDA's final determination.

sections.h2: Check the pharmacy before paying and separate product-status questions
paragraphs: The most reversible checkpoint occurs before a transaction. FDA's online-pharmacy guidance identifies state-board licensing as a sign of a safer legal pharmacy and provides BeSafeRx resources for license lookup. Before paying, identify the actual dispensing pharmacy, find its state-board record, compare legal names and locations, confirm that a valid prescription is required, and preserve the current offer terms. If the site hides the dispensing entity, offers prescription medicine without a valid prescription, or uses a license identity that doesn't match the transaction, stop the checkout review rather than treating a discount as compensation for missing evidence.

This doesn't turn Clinic Scout or a buyer into a pharmacy regulator. The checklist produces a documented channel decision. It can't prove the future contents of a shipment or guarantee that a licensed participant will never receive a counterfeit item. That is why post-delivery package and identifier checks still matter. It also can't determine whether a compounded semaglutide product is counterfeit Ozempic: a compounded product and an FDA-approved branded Ozempic product have different product-status questions. Don't use the Ozempic logo, active-ingredient name, or similar packaging language to erase that distinction.

Counterfeit is not a catch-all word for every product that is not an FDA-approved Ozempic pen. FDA's warning concerns products passed off as Ozempic and labeled with specific counterfeit information. A compounded semaglutide product is not FDA-approved Ozempic, but that product-status difference alone doesn't establish criminal counterfeiting. An illegally marketed product, a misbranded offer, a shipping error, and a package with a quality complaint can also require different evidence and reporting routes. Use the narrowest supported label in notes until a cited source makes a stronger determination.

This distinction prevents two failures. First, it avoids granting legitimacy to an offer that uses the word 'compounded' while imitating a branded product or hiding its pharmacy. Second, it avoids accusing a legitimate compounding pharmacy or seller of counterfeiting without evidence. Record exactly what the offer claimed, what the label says, what entity dispensed it, and whether the product was represented as Ozempic. FDA product-status and online-pharmacy resources can support separate checks, but the cited evidence does not decide regulatory classification for an individual transaction.

sections.h2: Build a traceable verification record
paragraphs: Use ten fields for each review: product as represented; physical product received; lot number; serial number; expiration and EXP/LOT placement; dispensing pharmacy legal name; state-board license record and check date; prescription and transaction record; FDA warning version and check date; contacts, submissions, and case numbers. Add a status beside each field: documented, missing, mismatched, or pending official response. This makes the record scannable and prevents one reassuring field from hiding several unanswered ones.

The checklist supports a decision to escalate, not a self-issued certificate. A package can have documented identifiers and still be pending manufacturer review. A pharmacy license can be valid while the source of one product remains under investigation. An FDA report can be accepted while the agency's determination remains open. Preserve those states. If facts change, append a dated update rather than rewriting the original entry. The goal is a traceable chain from offer to dispenser to physical package to official report, with uncertainty visible instead of edited away.

sections.h2: What a package check can and cannot conclude
paragraphs: Does a different lot number prove an Ozempic pen is authentic? No. It only means the package doesn't match that identifier from the current warning. Does the EXP/LOT position prove authenticity? No; it is one warning-specific visual check. Can a licensed pharmacy record authenticate a pen? No. It strengthens channel evidence. Should a warning-matching product be used, distributed, or sold? FDA says no. Can a seller's refund promise replace reporting? No. Preserve the transaction and use the official route appropriate to the product, pharmacy, adverse event, or suspected criminal activity.

Sources were checked through July 23, 2026: the FDA counterfeit Ozempic warning, FDA counterfeit-medicine guidance, and FDA BeSafeRx state-license resources. Reopen them for a real check because identifiers and instructions can change. It doesn't determine authenticity, diagnose exposure, attribute an adverse event, direct medical care, replace a pharmacist or regulator, or guarantee that a report will produce a particular outcome.
Readers comparing treatment goals can continue with [Ozempic alternatives](/best/ozempic-alternatives/).

sections.h2: Current official Wegovy tablet offers
paragraphs: The official Wegovy savings page reviewed August 2, 2026 listed $149 for one month of 1.5 mg tablets. It listed $149 for one month of 4 mg tablets through August 31, 2026, followed by $199 per month for 4 mg. One month is defined in the offer terms as one bottle of 30 tablets. Eligibility and restrictions apply, and Novo Nordisk says it may modify or cancel the program at any time.

The figures are manufacturer offer terms, not a universal retail price, insurance benefit, or guarantee of what every patient will pay. The same official page did not state a self-pay offer price for the 9 mg or 25 mg tablet doses in the terms captured for this review. That scoped finding means only that the amounts were not stated in the reviewed terms. It does not establish that no price exists elsewhere, and the 1.5 mg or 4 mg figures should not be extrapolated to those strengths.

For eligible commercially insured patients, the reviewed official page says patients may pay as little as $25 per month, subject to a maximum savings of $100 per month. Government beneficiaries are excluded, other restrictions apply, and “as little as” is not a guarantee. A current eligibility result and final pharmacy amount are still needed before treating the advertised floor as the amount due.

Read each amount together with its lane: self-pay or commercial insurance, exact tablet strength, one 30-tablet bottle, checked date, eligibility conditions, savings cap when applicable, and the manufacturer’s right to modify or cancel the program. Separating these fields preserves what the official terms establish without turning a conditional offer into a general price promise.

sections.h2: Why the amount may differ
paragraphs: A quoted manufacturer offer is only one part of the cost picture. The amount at checkout may depend on the tablet strength and point in the FDA-labeled escalation schedule, whether the patient qualifies for the current manufacturer offer, commercial insurance coverage, deductible, coinsurance, formulary rules, whether the plan requires prior authorization, the dispensing pharmacy, any fulfillment fees, and changes to offer terms after this article’s checked date.

Because the 4 mg offer has a dated change on August 31, 2026, any page that repeats the $149 amount after that date should be rechecked before relying on it. The checked date identifies when the cited page supported the statement; it does not freeze future terms. The official page and dispensing pharmacy are the appropriate places to verify a current amount.

A useful price record keeps the dosage form and strength beside the quote. It also keeps the offer type, one-month definition, eligibility restrictions, cap, deadline, and checked date beside the amount. Leaving out those qualifiers can make a source-accurate number misleading. This article therefore reports only the specific tablet terms the reviewed official page stated and leaves the 9 mg and 25 mg self-pay amounts as not stated in those terms.

sections.h2: What Wegovy tablets are
paragraphs: Wegovy tablets are FDA-approved, once-daily prescription tablets containing semaglutide. The FDA-approved tablet strengths are 1.5 mg, 4 mg, 9 mg, and 25 mg. The manufacturer describes the Wegovy pill as a once-daily prescription GLP-1 medication containing semaglutide. This identity and dosage-form summary comes from the current FDA prescribing information and the manufacturer’s official pill overview.

The current FDA prescribing information says Wegovy tablets are used with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight and at least one weight-related condition. The label also includes a cardiovascular-risk-reduction indication for certain adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight. Those population qualifiers are part of the label summary.

FDA approval does not make Wegovy an over-the-counter weight-loss product. Wegovy is available only by prescription, and a licensed clinician should determine whether it is appropriate for an individual. This page reports source-bound product, schedule, administration, safety, and offer facts; it does not make an individual treatment recommendation or predict whether a prescription will be issued.

sections.h2: FDA-approved tablet strengths and schedule
paragraphs: The FDA lists four Wegovy tablet strengths: 1.5 mg, 4 mg, 9 mg, and 25 mg. The labeled adult tablet schedule increases every 30 days: 1.5 mg once daily for days 1 through 30, 4 mg once daily for days 31 through 60, 9 mg once daily for days 61 through 90, and 25 mg once daily from day 91 onward.

The FDA says to start with 1.5 mg once daily for 30 days and identifies 25 mg once daily as the recommended maintenance dosage for adult weight reduction and cardiovascular-risk reduction. The schedule is a summary of the current label, not a personal dosing recommendation. A prescriber should give patient-specific instructions, including what to do if tolerability, other medicines, or health conditions affect treatment.

The dose schedule should not be used to infer price. The reviewed official offer stated self-pay amounts for 1.5 mg and 4 mg only. The captured terms did not state a self-pay amount for 9 mg or 25 mg. The presence of those strengths in the label establishes approved strengths and schedule, not a commercial amount for every bottle.

sections.h2: How the tablet is taken
paragraphs: According to the FDA prescribing information, Wegovy tablets should be taken once daily on an empty stomach in the morning, with water up to 4 ounces. The tablet should be swallowed whole, not split, crushed, chewed, or dissolved. After taking a tablet, the label says to wait at least 30 minutes before eating food, drinking beverages, or taking other oral medicines.

These administration statements summarize the label and are not personalized instructions. Administration matters because it can affect absorption, but a price article cannot determine what an individual should do with timing, tolerability, a missed dose, another medicine, or a health condition. Patients should follow the prescription label and their clinician’s instructions rather than changing timing or dose based on cost information.

sections.h2: Tablet cost versus injection cost
paragraphs: Wegovy tablets and Wegovy injections are different dosage forms with different strengths and administration schedules. Their manufacturer offers are also presented differently. The official page reviewed for this article listed tablet self-pay terms for 1.5 mg and 4 mg. It separately listed introductory and ongoing amounts for injection pens.

Injection pen prices should not be copied into a tablet-cost table, and the tablet offer should not be used to predict the price of an injection dose. When comparing forms, use the current price tied to the exact prescribed dosage form and strength. Clinical suitability is a separate decision for a licensed prescriber, and this article neither compares efficacy nor recommends one form over another.

A like-for-like check starts by confirming whether the prescription is for a tablet or injection, then recording the exact strength and quantity. It keeps the current official offer and final pharmacy amount attached to that exact product. This prevents a tablet amount, injection amount, introductory term, or recurring term from being presented as if it applied to a different transaction.

sections.h2: A five-step cost check before filling a prescription
paragraphs: First, confirm the exact dosage form and strength. Ask whether the prescription is for tablets or injection and which strength will be dispensed. Second, open the current official Wegovy price page because offer terms may change after this article’s checked date. Third, check eligibility before assuming an offer applies; the commercial-insurance offer excludes government beneficiaries and has a monthly savings cap.

Fourth, ask the insurance plan about coverage. Verify formulary status, prior authorization, deductible, and coinsurance for the exact product. Fifth, confirm the final amount with the pharmacy. The checkout amount, rather than an undated search result, is the number that matters. These steps organize a price check and do not determine coverage, eligibility, medical suitability, or a treatment choice.

Save the date and exact wording used for the price check. A dated manufacturer figure can be useful without being universal or permanent. If the strength, dosage form, insurance lane, eligibility, offer window, or pharmacy changes, recheck the amount rather than carrying an earlier figure forward. For the reviewed terms, keep the August 31, 2026 transition attached to the 4 mg $149 amount.

sections.h2: Safety and prescription-only boundary
paragraphs: The FDA prescribing information for Wegovy carries a boxed warning about the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. Wegovy is contraindicated for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2. The label also lists known hypersensitivity to semaglutide or any excipient in Wegovy tablets or injection as a contraindication.

The label says concomitant use of Wegovy tablets or injection with another semaglutide-containing product or another GLP-1 receptor agonist is not recommended. This statement preserves the label’s limitation-of-use boundary. It is not a medicine-reconciliation service and does not determine what any individual should start, stop, combine, or change.

This is not a complete safety summary. Read the current prescribing information and discuss risks, other medicines, pregnancy plans, symptoms, and medical history with a licensed clinician. The page does not promise efficacy, expected weight loss, comparative safety, suitability, availability, coverage, savings, or an individual outcome.

sections.h2: How to keep this price check current
paragraphs: Recheck the official sources when the dated 4 mg offer reaches August 31, 2026, when Novo Nordisk changes or cancels its savings terms, when FDA prescribing information changes, or when a new official price is published for the 9 mg or 25 mg tablets. A revision should preserve the same boundaries: exact dosage form and strength, offer lane, checked date, eligibility and cap language, and a clear distinction between a source’s silence and a universal claim.

Related Clinic Scout links provide context about manufacturer self-pay terms, savings-card conditions, and the separate safety evidence guide. They are informational internal links, not affiliate, checkout, contact, or provider-recommendation links.

This article answers a bounded question: what the reviewed official sources said about oral Wegovy strengths, labeled use and administration, key safety boundaries, and current dated offers. sections.heading: On this page
Mounjaro vs Ozempic: the short answer
paragraphs: Mounjaro contains tirzepatide, which acts at GIP and GLP-1 receptors. Ozempic contains semaglutide, which acts at the GLP-1 receptor. Both labels cover once-weekly prescription injections used with diet and exercise for type 2 diabetes, but the approved populations and risk-reduction indications are not identical. Neither Mounjaro nor Ozempic is FDA-approved under those brand names for weight loss. [S1][S2]

The strongest direct comparison is SURPASS-2, a 40-week open-label phase 3 trial in 1,879 adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes who were taking metformin. It compared tirzepatide 5, 10, and 15 mg with semaglutide 1 mg. That boundary matters: the trial did not compare tirzepatide with Ozempic's current 2 mg maximum dose, and an average trial result cannot identify the better medication for one person. [S1][S2][S3]

The practical answer depends on the treatment goal, current FDA indications, contraindications, tolerability, insurance rules, and the clinician's assessment. sections.heading: Mounjaro vs Ozempic at a glance

rows: What is the active ingredient?
Mounjaro is tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist. Ozempic is semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist. [S1][S2]
What are the brand labels for?

Both include glycemic control in type 2 diabetes. Ozempic also has specified cardiovascular and kidney-risk indications in adults; Mounjaro's current label includes patients age 10 and older. [S1][S2]
Is either brand approved for weight loss?
No. The current Mounjaro and Ozempic brand labels do not include a weight-management indication. [S1][S2]
What did the direct trial compare?
Tirzepatide 5, 10, or 15 mg versus semaglutide 1 mg for 40 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin. [S1][S3]
What are the displayed list prices?

As of August 2, 2026, Lilly displayed $1,112.16 per four-pen Mounjaro fill and NovoCare displayed $1,027.51 for Ozempic injection; the Ozempic quantity and supply period were not stated, so this is not a like-for-like comparison. [S4][S5]

sections.heading: 1. They use different active ingredients
paragraphs: Mounjaro's active ingredient is tirzepatide. Its label describes it as an agonist at both the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, or GIP, receptor and the glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1, receptor. Ozempic's active ingredient is semaglutide, and its label describes it as a GLP-1 receptor agonist. [S1][S2]

Both products are once-weekly injections. That shared cadence can make them look interchangeable in a search result, but their active ingredients, labeled dose ranges, approved populations, and precautions are distinct. They should not be treated as generic substitutes, and this guide provides no conversion or switching instructions. [S1][S2]

For readers comparing brand boundaries, the adjacent [Mounjaro versus Zepbound label-and-cost guide](/guides/mounjaro-vs-zepbound-label-and-cost/) explains why a shared ingredient does not make two brand labels identical. The same principle applies to semaglutide brands, as outlined in the [Ozempic versus Wegovy label-and-cost guide](/guides/ozempic-vs-wegovy-label-and-cost/).

sections.heading: 2. Their FDA-approved uses are not the same
paragraphs: Both labels include use with diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, but their full indication sections differ. Mounjaro is labeled for adults and pediatric patients age 10 and older with type 2 diabetes. Ozempic's current label is for adults and includes glycemic control plus specified risk-reduction indications for major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, and for sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, and cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. [S1][S2]

This is where many comparison pages blur separate products. Evidence from Zepbound or Wegovy should not be presented as though it changed the approved Mounjaro or Ozempic brand label. This guide therefore does not import obesity-trial percentages from those brands into the direct Mounjaro-versus-Ozempic comparison.

rows: Mounjaro glycemic-control population
Adults and pediatric patients age 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, as an adjunct to diet and exercise. [S1]
Ozempic glycemic-control population
Adults with type 2 diabetes, as an adjunct to diet and exercise. [S2]
Additional Ozempic indications

Specified cardiovascular-risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, plus specified kidney/cardiovascular-risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. [S2]
Weight-management indication under these brand names
Neither the Mounjaro nor Ozempic label establishes a weight-management indication for that brand. [S1][S2]

sections.heading: 3. The head-to-head trial favored tirzepatide—but only against semaglutide 1 mg
paragraphs: SURPASS-2 is more useful than comparing separate trials because it randomized participants within one study. The 40-week trial enrolled 1,879 adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes who were receiving metformin. Participants received tirzepatide 5, 10, or 15 mg, or semaglutide 1 mg. It was open-label. [S1][S3]

At week 40, mean A1C changes were -2.01, -2.24, and -2.30 percentage points with tirzepatide 5, 10, and 15 mg, compared with -1.86 percentage points with semaglutide 1 mg. Mean body-weight differences versus semaglutide favored the tirzepatide groups by 1.9, 3.6, and 5.5 kg. These are group averages from adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, not individual forecasts and not evidence that either brand is approved for weight loss. [S1][S3]

The missing 2 mg comparison is not a minor footnote. Ozempic's current label lists 0.5, 1, and 2 mg as maintenance doses based on glycemic control, while SURPASS-2 used semaglutide 1 mg. Saying only “Mounjaro beat Ozempic” strips away a key trial boundary. The accurate statement is narrower: tirzepatide at the studied doses produced larger average reductions than semaglutide 1 mg in the specified 40-week type 2 diabetes population. [S1][S2][S3]

headers: What it means for this comparison
rows: Population
Adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin; not a general weight-management population. [S3]
Duration
40 weeks; it does not answer every long-term effectiveness, persistence, or safety question. [S3]
Comparator
Semaglutide 1 mg, not Ozempic's current 2 mg maximum maintenance dose. [S1][S2][S3]
Result
Tirzepatide groups had larger average A1C reductions and weight changes than semaglutide 1 mg in this trial. [S1][S3]
What it cannot prove
A universal winner, a personal outcome, a direct comparison with semaglutide 2 mg, or a weight-loss indication for Mounjaro or Ozempic. [S1][S2][S3]

sections.heading: 4. The available dose ranges differ
paragraphs: The Mounjaro adult label spans strengths from 2.5 mg through 15 mg. It states that 2.5 mg is used for initiation and is not intended for glycemic control, and it lists 15 mg once weekly as the adult maximum. The pediatric maximum in the current label is 10 mg once weekly. Ozempic's label uses 0.25 mg for initiation and lists 0.5, 1, or 2 mg as maintenance doses based on glycemic control. [S1][S2]
Before inferring monthly cost from a sticker price, verify the prescribed presentation, package dose count, pharmacy availability, plan approval, and billing unit.

sections.heading: 5. Side effects overlap, but label details matter
paragraphs: Both current labels carry a boxed warning stating that the drug caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents and that it is unknown whether it causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, in humans. [S1][S2]

Both labels list contraindications involving a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2, and serious hypersensitivity to the product or its components. Those boundaries require clinician review; a comparison article cannot screen someone for them. [S1][S2]

Common gastrointestinal adverse reactions overlap. Mounjaro's label lists nausea, diarrhea, decreased appetite, vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain among reactions reported in at least 5% of treated patients. Ozempic's label lists nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation among reactions reported in at least 5% of treated patients. Different wording or percentages across labels and studies should not be simplified into a claim that one drug is universally safer or easier to tolerate. [S1][S2]

The Mounjaro label contains a specific precaution about oral hormonal contraceptives after initiation and after dose escalation. Review that instruction and the complete current medication list with a clinician or pharmacist rather than making self-directed changes. [S1]

sections.heading: 6. List prices and what your plan can change
paragraphs: As of August 2, 2026, Lilly's official pricing page displayed a Mounjaro list price of $1,112.16 per fill and defined a fill as four pens. NovoCare displayed an Ozempic injection list price of $1,027.51. These are manufacturer reference prices, not a forecast of what any patient will pay. [S4][S5]

We read these list prices directly from the manufacturers' official pricing pages—Lilly for Mounjaro and NovoCare for Ozempic—on the date shown; we do not use coupon sites, aggregator price trackers, or pharmacy estimates.

The official Ozempic page did not state the package quantity or supply period represented by its displayed price, so subtracting the two figures would not be a like-for-like comparison. The right comparison is the current plan-and-pharmacy result for the exact prescription—not list price alone. [S4][S5]

For a reusable estimate, the [GLP-1 cost calculator](/tools/glp-1-cost-calculator/) can organize price inputs without claiming that an estimate is a pharmacy quote. Recheck the manufacturer's official pricing and savings pages at click time, especially because this article's price evidence is dated.

rows: Manufacturer list price
Mounjaro: $1,112.16 per four-pen fill; Ozempic injection: $1,027.51 as displayed August 2, 2026. Recheck both official pages because prices can change. [S4][S5]
Insurance coverage

Confirm with the plan how your insurance benefit sets the out-of-pocket cost for this exact prescription, because the manufacturer states the pharmacy price largely depends on insurer-set out-of-pocket costs, pharmacy charges, and any discounts or financial assistance. [S4][S5]
Pharmacy claim
Ask for the price for the exact product, strength, presentation, quantity, and days' supply after the pharmacy runs the current claim.
Savings program
Read the manufacturer's current savings terms before assuming any discount: eligibility and restrictions apply, and the offer is subject to change or discontinuation at any time without notice. [S6]

sections.heading: 7. The better fit depends on the clinical goal
paragraphs: The labels create different evidence lanes. A clinician considering glycemic control may weigh the SURPASS-2 findings, but must keep the semaglutide 1 mg comparator and the trial population in view. A clinician evaluating a person with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease may also consider the additional risk-reduction indications in Ozempic's current label. Pediatric eligibility differs because Mounjaro's label includes patients age 10 and older while Ozempic's current label is for adults. [S1][S2][S3]

Coverage can dominate an otherwise reasonable clinical comparison. Before treating either option as accessible, verify whether the plan covers the exact brand for the relevant diagnosis and what documentation is required. If coverage is absent or the claim price is not sustainable, ask the clinician and plan about lawful covered alternatives rather than relying on an unverified coupon headline.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before choosing
ordered_items: Which current FDA-labeled indication is relevant to my diagnosis and treatment goal?
Do any boxed warnings, contraindications, precautions, interactions, or current medicines change the options for me?
How should the SURPASS-2 semaglutide 1 mg comparator affect how we interpret the results for my situation?
Does my plan cover the exact brand for my diagnosis, and does it require prior authorization or step therapy?
What will the exact prescription cost after the pharmacy runs a current claim?
What follow-up and monitoring does my clinician recommend?
If the preferred product is unavailable or unaffordable, what covered alternatives should we discuss?

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: Mounjaro and Ozempic share a weekly type 2 diabetes context, but they are not interchangeable. Tirzepatide produced larger average A1C and weight changes than semaglutide 1 mg in the bounded SURPASS-2 trial, while Ozempic's label includes additional cardiovascular and kidney-risk indications in specified adults. Mounjaro's label includes pediatric patients age 10 and older. [S1][S2][S3]

Use those differences to frame a clinician and insurance conversation—not to declare a universal winner. Verify the current labels, contraindications, exact pharmacy claim, and manufacturer terms before acting. This article is educational and does not diagnose, prescribe, determine eligibility, or replace a licensed professional.

Labels and prices were last checked August 2, 2026.

claims.statement: The lowest official amount verified is a $50 copay through the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge for eligible Part D beneficiaries, not a universal retail price.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge runs from July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027, operates outside the normal Part D payment flow, and has specific cost-accounting rules.
The Bridge currently covers Foundayo, Wegovy tablets and injection, and Zepbound KwikPen when used for the weight-management indication; single-dose Zepbound vial and pen formulations are excluded.
NovoCare lists Wegovy tablets at $149 for 1.5 mg, a time-limited $149 then $199 for 4 mg, and $299 for 9 mg and 25 mg; it separately lists limited first-fill and standard injection prices.
The current Wegovy label identifies the tablet indication, tablet starting and maintenance strengths, injection starting dosage, and adult injection maintenance strengths.
LillyDirect lists Foundayo at $149 for 0.8 mg, $199 for 2.5 mg, and $299 for 5.5 mg through 17.2 mg, with a 45-day refill condition and $349 regular price at 14.5 mg and 17.2 mg.
The current Foundayo label identifies orforglipron as an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist for long-term weight reduction and states its starting and later dosage levels.

LillyDirect lists Zepbound at $299 for the 2.5 mg starting dose, $399 for 5 mg, and $449 at higher listed strengths when refilled within 45 days, with higher regular prices if the condition is missed.
The current Zepbound label identifies tirzepatide as a GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, 2.5 mg as the starting dosage, and 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg as weight-reduction maintenance dosages.
Manufacturer programs use different supply-period definitions and carry eligibility, timing, limit, and modification terms.

FDA has reported dosing-error adverse events involving compounded injectable semaglutide and urges consumers buying online to use state-licensed pharmacies.
A medication-only manufacturer price does not by itself establish total program cost; the article uses an explicit additive worksheet and routes provider-fee comparisons to existing cluster pages.

sections.heading: The short price answer
paragraphs: Searching for the **cheapest GLP-1** usually produces numbers that are not directly comparable. One page may show an insured copay. Another may advertise only an introductory dose. A telehealth program may quote a care fee without medication. A compounded product may sit beside an FDA-approved medicine even though the FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness, or quality before marketing. [S9]

This guide uses a narrower method. We checked current FDA prescribing information, official manufacturer self-pay pages, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services on August 3, 2026. We compare FDA-approved weight-management products and official access paths only. We do not rank telehealth providers, recommend a medicine, or treat a starting price as a long-term price.

Every product compared here is a prescription-only medicine: none of these prices is available without a valid prescription from a licensed clinician, and the manufacturer program, plan, or pharmacy must also accept it. [S2] [S4] [S6]

The lowest official number we verified is the **$50 copay** under the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. It is not available to everyone. CMS describes it as a temporary program for eligible Medicare Part D beneficiaries, running from July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2027. The drugs must be prescribed for weight management, and the eligible list currently includes Foundayo, Wegovy tablets and injection, and Zepbound KwikPen. [S7] [S8]

For self-pay access outside that program, current official pages show **$149 starting prices** for Wegovy tablets and Foundayo. Those headline prices are attached to starting or early strengths. The current FDA labels identify Wegovy 25 mg as the tablet maintenance dose, while Foundayo begins at 0.8 mg and may move through higher strengths based on response and tolerability. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4]

At the labeled maintenance level, the lowest official self-pay amount we verified is $299 per month. Intermediate titration strengths can cost less: LillyDirect lists Foundayo 2.5 mg at $199 per 30-day month. NovoCare lists Wegovy 25 mg tablets at $299 per month. LillyDirect lists Foundayo 5.5 mg and 9 mg at $299, and 14.5 mg and 17.2 mg at $299 when the refill-timing condition is met. Those are prices, not treatment recommendations; a prescriber determines whether a product and labeled strength are appropriate. [S1] [S3] [S4]

The table answers the literal price question while preserving the qualifiers. It does not prove which medicine will cost least for one person. Insurance benefits, program eligibility, prescription decisions, refill timing, needles, clinician fees, laboratory charges, and shipping can change the actual total.

sections.heading: What “cheapest” must include
ordered_items: **Medicare Bridge copay.** A narrow federal demonstration with eligibility and clinical criteria, not an ordinary retail cash price. [S7] [S8]
**Manufacturer self-pay price.** A price offered under manufacturer terms, often outside insurance and subject to change. [S1] [S3] [S5]
**Introductory price.** A number limited to a starting strength, new patient, first fills, or expiration date. [S1] [S3] [S5]
**Later-dose or maintenance price.** The amount attached to a strength used after initiation or identified in the label as maintenance. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5] [S6]
**Total program cost.** Medication plus care, membership, labs, supplies, shipping, and other required charges.
paragraphs: A useful comparison needs one consistent unit. We use the official page's defined month or supply period, identify the strength tied to each number, and separate five payment lanes:

That last lane is where many “from” prices break. A medication price is not automatically a telehealth program total. Before comparing providers, use our [full GLP-1 program cost method](/guides/glp-1-program-total-cost-comparison/) and [line-by-line provider fee worksheet](/guides/compare-online-glp-1-provider-fees/). They handle the costs this product-level guide intentionally does not rank.

We include a number only when an official current source states the amount and its key qualifier. We attach the number to a specific product, formulation, strength, and access program. We do not convert a starting offer into an annual average. We do not assume a higher strength will be prescribed. We do not subtract a coupon without documented eligibility. We mark compounded products as a separate regulatory lane rather than using them to declare a winner.
The result is deliberately less dramatic than an affiliate leaderboard. It is also more useful: the lowest visible number appears beside the condition that makes it true.

sections.heading: Wegovy official self-pay prices
paragraphs: Wegovy is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Its current FDA label indicates WEGOVY tablets, with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term in adults with obesity or adults with overweight and at least one weight-related comorbid condition; the label also covers WEGOVY injection, whose adult weight-reduction maintenance dosages are 1.7 mg or 2.4 mg, with 2.4 mg recommended. [S2]
For tablets, the FDA label identifies **1.5 mg once daily as the starting dosage** and **25 mg once daily as the maintenance dosage**. The label also lists 4 mg and 9 mg tablet strengths. [S2]

That makes “Wegovy for $149” true but incomplete. The $149 figure belongs to 1.5 mg and a time-limited 4 mg offer. It should not be described as the continuing price for the 25 mg maintenance strength. [S1] [S2]

For injection, NovoCare lists $199 per month for patients new to the Wegovy Savings Offer and NovoCare Pharmacy at 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg, for the first two monthly fills through December 31, 2026. Its price guide then lists $349 per month for the 0.25 mg through 2.4 mg strengths and $399 for Wegovy HD 7.2 mg. The FDA label identifies 1.7 mg or 2.4 mg as adult weight-reduction maintenance strengths, with 2.4 mg recommended. [S1] [S2]

Novo Nordisk states that eligibility and restrictions apply and reserves the right to modify or cancel the program. A month for the injection offer is one box of four pens. Those conditions belong next to the price, not in invisible fine print. [S1]

sections.heading: Foundayo official self-pay prices
paragraphs: Foundayo contains orforglipron and is an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist. The current FDA label indicates it for long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight and at least one weight-related comorbid condition, with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. [S4]

The label starts at 0.8 mg once daily, moves to 2.5 mg after at least 30 days, then to 5.5 mg after at least another 30 days. It allows later increases to 9 mg, 14.5 mg, or 17.2 mg based on treatment response and tolerability. This is label context, not a self-directed instruction; medication changes belong with the prescriber. [S4]

Foundayo shows why a starting price and a later-treatment price must be separated. The $149 headline is tied to the 0.8 mg starting strength. The verified later strengths begin at $199 for 2.5 mg and reach $299 from 5.5 mg upward. The two highest listed strengths keep the $299 amount only when the Journey Program refill timing is met. [S3] [S4]

Lilly states that eligibility is required, savings are subject to monthly and annual limits, the program is not insurance, and terms may be changed or ended. The manufacturer defines a month as 30 days on this page. [S3]

sections.heading: Zepbound official self-pay prices
paragraphs: Zepbound contains tirzepatide, a GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist. Its current FDA label indicates it for long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight and at least one weight-related comorbid condition, with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. [S6]

The label identifies 2.5 mg once weekly for four weeks as the starting dosage. For weight reduction and long-term maintenance, it lists 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg once weekly. LillyDirect separately states that 2.5 mg is not approved as a maintenance dose. [S5] [S6]

Higher listed strengths show a lower Journey Program amount when refilled within 45 days and a higher regular price when that condition is missed. [S5] [S6]
Lilly defines the program month as 28 days and one single-patient-use KwikPen. It also says a pen-needle purchase is required. Eligibility, monthly and annual limits, and changing terms apply. [S5]

sections.heading: The $50 Medicare GLP-1 Bridge
paragraphs: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge is the lowest official out-of-pocket number in this comparison, but it is also the narrowest access path. CMS says the program runs from July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2027, for eligible Medicare Part D beneficiaries. Eligible beneficiaries have a $50 copay. [S7]
CMS currently lists these products when used for weight management:

The program operates outside the normal Part D coverage and payment flow. CMS states that the Part D deductible does not apply, the $50 does not count toward true out-of-pocket costs, and the low-income subsidy is not added to that copay. [S7]

Eligibility is not established by having Part D alone. CMS's provider page sets out the clinical criteria for the Bridge, including that the drug be prescribed for weight management and used with current and ongoing lifestyle modification including structured nutrition and physical activity consistent with the FDA-approved label; a clinician and the program determine whether the criteria are met. [S8]

For a reader who may qualify, the accurate next step is to check the current CMS criteria and work through the prescription and program-eligibility process. It is not accurate to advertise “GLP-1s cost $50 with Medicare” without the Part D, product, indication, clinical-criteria, and program-period boundaries.

sections.heading: Why compounded prices stay separate
paragraphs: Top-ranking pages for this query include affiliate provider rankings that list compounded products beside FDA-approved medicines. We do not use those amounts to declare the cheapest FDA-approved GLP-1.

FDA states that unapproved versions do not undergo its review for safety, effectiveness, and quality before marketing. It also states that compounded drugs are not FDA approved and should be used only when a patient's medical needs cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug. [S9]

FDA reports adverse events, some requiring hospitalization, that may be related to dosing errors with compounded injectable semaglutide products; it also notes that injectable GLP-1 drugs require refrigeration as indicated in their package inserts and urges consumers buying medicine online to purchase only from state-licensed pharmacies. [S9]

That does not mean every compounded prescription is unlawful or that a general article can decide what one patient needs. It means the comparison must preserve the regulatory difference. A compounded-product quote belongs in a separate conversation with the prescriber and pharmacy, not in a table that implies equivalence to Foundayo, Wegovy, or Zepbound.

sections.heading: A safe comparison checklist
ordered_items: **Confirm the treatment lane.** Is the number for an FDA-approved weight-management product, an off-label product, or a compounded drug? Do not merge those categories. [S2] [S4] [S6] [S9]
**Confirm the formulation.** Tablet, single-dose pen, vial, and KwikPen can have different prices and program rules. [S1] [S5] [S8]
**Confirm the strength.** Ask whether the advertised price belongs only to initiation or also applies at the labeled later or maintenance strength. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5] [S6]

**Confirm the supply period.** NovoCare defines a month for the Wegovy injection offer as one box of four pens, the Zepbound program month is 28 days and one single-patient-use KwikPen, and the Foundayo page defines a 30-day month. [S1] [S3] [S5]

**Confirm eligibility.** Self-pay, commercial insurance, and Medicare Bridge are different rails. A valid prescription or plan membership does not by itself prove program acceptance. [S3] [S5] [S7] [S8]
**Confirm the post-offer price.** Record the date or fill when the price changes and the amount that replaces it. [S1] [S3] [S5]
**Add required fees.** Include care, membership, labs, supplies, needles, shipping, and pharmacy charges.
**Save the source and date.** Prices and program rules are volatile. A screenshot without a date and terms is not durable evidence.

claims.statement: The current Zepbound coupon landscape has separate commercial covered, commercial noncovered, cash self-pay, and Medicare Bridge lanes; the headline amounts cannot be applied universally.

Eligible commercially insured patients with coverage for the Zepbound single-dose pen may pay as little as $25 for a qualifying one-, two-, or three-month fill, with per-fill caps, an annual maximum up to $1,300, up to 13 fills, HIPAA authorization, and a current 2026-12-31 end date.
The commercial card excludes enrollment in listed state, federal, or government-funded healthcare programs and requires United States or Puerto Rico residency and age 18 or older.

For eligible commercially insured patients whose plan does not cover Zepbound, the current terms list as low as $499 for a one-month single-dose-pen fill and dose-specific KwikPen amounts of $299, $399, or $449.

The higher-strength KwikPen $449 purchase offer applies to the first eligible purchase and requires a subsequent purchase within 45 days of prior delivery or receipt to continue; listed regular prices can apply when the condition is missed.

The KwikPen self-pay card is for eligible cash-paying patients, requires a qualifying prescription, U.S. or Puerto Rico residency, and age 18 or older, and bars third-party reimbursement or deductible/true-out-of-pocket credit.
Current KwikPen self-pay terms list $299 for 2.5 mg, $399 for 5 mg, and $449 for 7.5 mg through 15 mg, define a month as 28 days and one KwikPen, permit up to 11 fills in 2026, and end on 2026-12-31.

Lilly lists a Zepbound list-price range of $499 to $1,086.37 per fill and says the final pharmacy amount depends on insurance out-of-pocket rules, pharmacy charges, discounts, and financial assistance.

LillyDirect says the Zepbound vial is available through LillyDirect self-pay with home delivery or Walmart Pharmacy pickup and that Zepbound requires a valid prescription from a licensed healthcare provider.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge runs from July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027, operates outside the ordinary Part D payment flow, and has a $50 copay for eligible beneficiaries.
Under the current CMS product list, Zepbound KwikPen is eligible through the Bridge for weight management when criteria are met, while Zepbound single-dose vial and single-dose pen are excluded.

The current FDA-approved Zepbound label states its approved weight-reduction and obstructive-sleep-apnea uses, carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors, and lists MTC/MEN 2 contraindications.

The current Lilly cards require activation where stated, prohibit combining savings with another Zepbound discount or coupon, state that the cards are not insurance, and allow Lilly to change or end terms.

The existing cross-brand savings-card page remains the Zepbound-versus-Wegovy terms-comparison owner, while this new route owns the exact 2026 Zepbound coupon lookup, current numeric matrix, and transaction workflow.
The publication transaction adds differentiated contextual inbound links from the existing cross-brand savings-card page and cheapest-GLP-1 guide to the exact new route.

sections.heading: Start with the four current payment lanes
paragraphs: The lowest number is not the first fact to check. Start with the payer category, coverage response, prescribed presentation, and transaction route. The current official terms produce four distinct paths.

These lanes cannot be collapsed into “Zepbound costs $25” or “Zepbound costs $299.” The commercial card excludes enrollment in listed government-funded programs. The self-pay card operates outside insurance and prohibits reimbursement. The CMS Bridge is not the commercial card. The final pharmacy amount can also differ because insurance cost sharing, pharmacy charges, available assistance, and transaction details vary. [S1] [S2] [S3]

If you want the broader cross-brand framework, read the [Zepbound and Wegovy savings-card terms comparison](/guides/zepbound-wegovy-savings-card-terms/). This page stays narrower: the exact Zepbound offer and the exact fill being priced.

If you are comparing a provider route separately from the manufacturer card, the existing Shed provider record is available here: [Shed provider record](https://track.revoffers.com/aff_c?offer_id=1516&aff_id=13031). That tracked route is not evidence that a coupon applies, that a prescription will be issued, or that any total price, shipping term, coverage result, or clinical outcome is guaranteed.

sections.heading: Understand what “Zepbound coupon” means
paragraphs: The manufacturer calls its main commercial offer a savings card. Searchers often call it a coupon. That label is workable only if the underlying program is named. A Lilly commercial card, a Lilly cash self-pay card, a pharmacy discount card, an insurer copay, and the Medicare Bridge are different payment mechanisms. They can have different eligibility, claims processing, device coverage, refill limits, and accounting treatment.

The commercial card requires activation and cannot be combined with another discount, coupon, incentive, or similar Zepbound offer. Lilly states that the card is not insurance and reserves the right to amend or end eligibility and terms. Current commercial savings end on December 31, 2026. [S1]

The cash self-pay card is also not insurance. It is for cash-paying patients and bars seeking reimbursement from private insurance, a government program, or another third-party payer. Under its terms, the amount cannot be applied to a deductible or true out-of-pocket obligation. That can make a lower checkout amount financially useful while still producing no progress toward an insurance threshold. [S2]

A generic pharmacy discount card is outside this evidence set. Its presence in search results does not prove manufacturer eligibility, and a manufacturer amount does not predict what an unrelated discount card will quote. Compare one fully identified route at a time, then ask the dispensing pharmacy for the final amount before payment.

sections.heading: Commercial insurance with Zepbound coverage
paragraphs: The $25 headline belongs to a specific lane. Current Lilly terms say an adult in the United States or Puerto Rico must have a prescription consistent with the FDA-approved labeling, be enrolled in a commercial drug plan that covers the Zepbound single-dose pen, and not be enrolled in listed government-funded healthcare programs. A valid patient HIPAA authorization is also required. [S1]

“As little as $25” is a floor after conditions, not a promise that the card will erase every balance. Suppose the plan’s remaining patient responsibility exceeds the program’s maximum assistance for that fill. The patient may owe more than $25 because the assistance cap—not the headline—limits what the card can contribute. The pharmacy’s adjudicated result is therefore the decision-bearing number.

The supply period matters too. Do not multiply the one-month maximum by three and assume every three-month prescription will process that way. The current terms set separate savings caps for 1-, 2-, and 3-month fills. Ask the pharmacy whether the submitted product and quantity match the current card definition. Save the offer version and receipt so a later difference can be traced to the plan response, quantity, remaining benefit, or program terms. [S1]

Commercial insurance is not a sufficient label by itself. The plan must cover the prescribed single-dose pen for this $25 lane. A plan can be commercial yet return a noncovered response. That moves the transaction to a different set of terms rather than turning the covered amount into a standing cash price.

The 45-day condition is a purchase-timing rule, not a clinical instruction. Do not change treatment timing to preserve a commercial price. If an authorized prescriber changes the plan or a fill is delayed, ask Lilly or the pharmacy what amount applies; keep the medical decision separate from the discount.

Cash self-pay may be cheaper at checkout than another available route, but the comparison is incomplete until insurance accounting is considered. If the terms say the purchase will not count toward a deductible, include that lost progress in the household budget. The [GLP-1 total-cost method](/guides/glp-1-program-total-cost-comparison/) can help separate medication, clinician, membership, laboratory, supply, shipping, and other charges without pretending every line is present in every transaction.

sections.heading: Medicare and other government benefits use a different path
paragraphs: The Lilly commercial savings card excludes people enrolled in Medicare, Medicare Part D, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, VA, DoD, TRICARE, and other listed government-funded programs. That exclusion does not mean every Medicare beneficiary lacks an access route. It means the commercial card is the wrong program to quote. [S1]

CMS launched the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge for eligible Part D beneficiaries from July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2027. The Bridge operates outside the ordinary Part D coverage and payment flow, and eligible beneficiaries have a $50 copay. CMS requires eligible plan enrollment, use for weight management, and satisfaction of its clinical criteria. [S6] [S7]

For Zepbound, CMS currently lists KwikPen as an eligible Bridge product when used to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction. The Zepbound single-dose vial and single-dose pen are not available through the Bridge. The $50 figure therefore cannot be attached to every Zepbound prescription, presentation, indication, or Medicare beneficiary. [S7]

If Medicare is involved, use the CMS eligibility route rather than trying to force the commercial card. Ask the prescriber and plan which indication and product presentation are being processed and whether the Bridge criteria apply. This article does not screen an individual against those criteria.
For a broader explanation of why assistance is not the same as plan coverage, see [GLP-1 insurance support versus coverage](/guides/glp-1-insurance-support-vs-coverage/).

sections.heading: Activate and use the correct offer without guessing
ordered_items: **Name the payer category.** Record commercial insurance, Medicare, another government benefit, or cash self-pay. If more than one benefit exists, ask the plan or program how it affects eligibility rather than selecting the cheapest label.
**Copy the exact presentation.** Distinguish the single-dose pen, single-dose vial, and single-patient-use KwikPen. Do not reduce all three to “pen.”
**Obtain the coverage response.** For commercial insurance, ask whether the plan covers the exact presentation on the prescription and what patient responsibility remains after adjudication.
**Open the current official program.** Use Lilly’s Zepbound savings page and select the matching category. Read the full terms, not only the headline card.

**Confirm the bounded fields.** Check advertised floor, maximum assistance, supply definition, remaining fills, higher-strength timing if relevant, expiration, and whether the purchase operates inside or outside insurance.

**Activate the card if required.** Lilly’s commercial terms state that activation is required. Keep the card details private and provide them only through the official program and pharmacy workflow. [S1]

**Ask the pharmacy to process the identified lane.** Request the final amount before authorizing payment. If insurance is part of the commercial route, confirm whether the plan response was processed before the manufacturer benefit.
**Save a dated record.** Keep the terms version, coverage response, receipt, and any program or pharmacy explanation. Do not post member, prescription, card, or diagnosis information publicly.
